stories.title: Cherokee removal and the Trail of Tears
facts: The Indian Removal Act of 28 May 1830 let the President negotiate treaties to move tribes living east of the Mississippi to land in the west.
https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/jacksons-message-to-congress-on-indian-removal

In December 1835 a small group of Cherokee men, none of them elected officials of the Nation, signed the Treaty of New Echota, giving up all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi for $5 million and land in Indian Territory.
https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/cherokee-resistance-and-relocation.htm
Principal Chief John Ross gathered more than 15,000 signatures, nearly the whole Nation, asking the Senate not to ratify it.
https://www.ncpedia.org/cherokee/trailoftears
The Senate ratified the treaty in 1836 by a single vote.
https://www.nps.gov/liri/learn/historyculture/the-trail-of-tears.htm
In May 1838 federal troops and state militias began rounding up Cherokee families into stockades; the forced journey west ran from October 1838 to March 1839.
https://www.nps.gov/liri/learn/historyculture/the-trail-of-tears.htm
More than 16,000 Cherokee people were removed to Indian Territory (now Oklahoma), travelling in 17 detachments along routes of about 2,200 miles.
https://www.nps.gov/places/trail-of-tears-national-historic-trail.htm
A few hundred stayed by hiding in the North Carolina mountains; their descendants are the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians.
https://www.ncpedia.org/cherokee/trailoftears

voices.text: But we were doubly grieved when we understood, from a letter of the Secretary of War to our Delegation, dated March of the present year, that our father the President had refused us protection, and that he had decided in favor of the extension of the laws of the State over us. This decision induces us to appeal to the immediate representatives of the American people. We love, we dearly love our country, and it is due to your honorable bodies as well as to us, to make known why we think the country is ours, and why we wish to remain in peace where we are.
voices.who: The Cherokee Nation, memorial to the U.S. Congress

voices.text: By the stipulations of this instrument, we are despoiled of our private possessions, the indefeasible property of individuals. We are stripped of every attribute of freedom and eligibility for legal self-defence. Our property may be plundered before our eyes; violence may be committed on our persons; even our lives may be taken away, and there is none to regard our complaints. We are denationalized; we are disfranchised. We are deprived of membership in the human family! We have neither land nor home, nor resting place that can be called our own. And this is effected by the provisions of a compact which assumes the venerated, the sacred appellation of treaty.
voices.who: Principal Chief John Ross, protest to the Senate and House of Representatives against the Treaty of New Echota
voices.doc: as printed by the U.S. National Park Service

official.text: It gives me pleasure to announce to Congress that the benevolent policy of the Government, steadily pursued for nearly thirty years, in relation to the removal of the Indians beyond the white settlements is approaching to a happy consummation.
official.who: President Andrew Jackson, message to Congress 'On Indian Removal'

disputed: How many died. About 4,000, nearly a fifth of the Cherokee, is the figure most sources give; it goes back to the missionary doctor Elizur Butler. The National Park Service writes that no one knows how many died throughout the ordeal.
stories.blind: Most of what survives is the writing of literate Cherokee leaders, missionaries and army officers. Ordinary Cherokee people, especially women and children and those who spoke only Cherokee, are heard mostly in recollections written down much later.
reading: Trail of Tears National Historic Trail: bibliography (NPS)
Petition against the Treaty of New Echota (National Archives, DocsTeach)

stories.title: Rubber and terror in the Congo Free State
stories.where: Lake Tumba region, Équateur, today's Democratic Republic of the Congo (representative location)
facts: The Berlin Conference of 1884–85 recognised the Congo Free State, ruled personally by King Leopold II of Belgium.
https://www.britannica.com/place/Congo-Free-State
Congolese people were forced to gather wild rubber, palm oil and ivory; families were taken hostage to enforce quotas, and soldiers of the Force Publique cut off hands, including children's.
https://www.britannica.com/place/Congo-Free-State
The British consul Roger Casement travelled the Upper Congo in 1903; his report, dated 11 December 1903, was laid before Parliament in February 1904 as Command Paper Cd. 1933.
https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/50573/pg50573-images.html
Casement and E. D. Morel founded the Congo Reform Association in 1904.
https://breac.nd.edu/articles/the-three-lives-of-the-casement-report-its-impact-on-official-reactions-and-popular-opinion-in-belgium/
The Free State's own Commission of Inquiry, in the Congo from October 1904 to February 1905, confirmed the abuses.
https://breac.nd.edu/articles/the-three-lives-of-the-casement-report-its-impact-on-official-reactions-and-popular-opinion-in-belgium/
Under international pressure Belgium took the territory over in 1908 as the Belgian Congo.
https://breac.nd.edu/articles/the-three-lives-of-the-casement-report-its-impact-on-official-reactions-and-popular-opinion-in-belgium/

voices.text: We had to go further and further into the forest to find the rubber vines, to go without food, and our women had to give up cultivating the fields and gardens. Then we starved. Wild beasts—the leopards—killed some of us when we were working away in the forest, and others got lost or died from exposure and starvation, and we begged the white man to leave us alone, saying we could get no more rubber, but the white men and their soldiers said: ‘Go! You are only beasts yourselves, you are nyama (meat).’ We tried, always going further into the forest, and when we failed and our rubber was short, the soldiers came to our towns and killed us. Many were shot, some had their ears cut off; others were tied up with ropes around their necks and bodies and taken away.
voices.who: A refugee from the rubber tax (named only as “N N” in the published report), speaking to Roger Casement
voices.doc: Correspondence and Report from His Majesty's Consul at Boma (Cd. 1933, 1904), Inclosure 1 in No. 3

voices.text: We said to the white men, ‘We are not enough people now to do what you want us. Our country has not many people in it and we are dying fast. We are killed by the work you make us do, by the stoppage of our plantations, and the breaking up of our homes.’ The white man looked at us and said: ‘There are lots of people in Mputu’
voices.who: Another refugee in the same group (“P P” in the report); Casement notes that Mputu meant Europe

official.text: They deny, however, that the manner in which the State is administered involves a systematic régime “of cruelty or oppression,”
official.who: The Congo Free State's government: a note to the Powers that signed the Berlin Act, signed by its Secretary-General, Chevalier de Cuvelier, in Brussels (English translation printed in the same Parliamentary paper)

disputed: How many died. Adam Hochschild's widely read estimate is about 10 million, from a population he argues was roughly halved between 1880 and 1920. The demographer Jean-Paul Sanderson told the Belgian Parliament's Congo commission in 2022 that the starting population was probably 11.5 to 15 million, and traced the 10-million figure to Mark Twain's writing in 1908. Administrative counts began in the late 1800s, but Sanderson considers them reliable only from about 1935.

Deaths or decline. Sanderson attributes the fall mainly to higher mortality and lower birth rates, from violence, flight, famine and diseases such as sleeping sickness, and stresses that the gap measures decline, not violent deaths alone; Britannica reports a decline said to be from some 20 million to 8 million.
stories.blind: Congolese voices survive only as answers given to European questioners, through interpreters, and printed with names removed. The dead, most women, and people who never met a missionary or consul are almost entirely missing.
reading: The three lives of the Casement Report (University of Notre Dame, Breac)

stories.title: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre
facts: On 13 April 1919 troops under General Dyer fired on a large unarmed crowd in the Jallianwala Bagh, a walled garden in Amritsar; Dyer reported that his party fired 1,650 rounds.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/lords/1920/jul/19/punjab-disturbances-the-case-of-general
In the House of Commons the Secretary for War, Winston Churchill, gave the official toll as 379 killed and at least 1,200 wounded, and called it a monstrous event.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1920/jul/08/army-council-and-general-dyer
Martial law followed in the Punjab, enforced with public floggings and other humiliations; Rabindranath Tagore gave up the knighthood he had received in 1915.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Jallianwala-Bagh-Massacre

The government's Disorders Inquiry (Hunter) Committee condemned General Dyer's conduct; on 8 July 1920 the Commons rejected, by 230 votes to 129, Sir Edward Carson's motion protesting at his treatment.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1920/jul/08/army-council-and-general-dyer
On 20 July 1920 the House of Lords voted 129 to 86 for a motion deploring the handling of General Dyer's case as unjust to him.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/lords/1920/jul/20/punjab-disturbances-the-case-of-general

voices.text: The enormity of the measures taken by the Government in the Punjab for quelling some local disturbances has, with a rude shock, revealed to our minds the helplessness of our position as British subjects in India. The disproportionate severity of the punishments inflicted upon the unfortunate people and the methods of carrying them out, we are convinced, are without parallel in the history of civilised governments, barring some conspicuous exceptions, recent and remote. Considering that such treatment has been meted out to a population, disarmed and resourceless, by a power which has the most terribly efficient organisation for destruction of human lives, we must strongly assert that it can claim no political expediency, far less moral justification.
voices.who: Rabindranath Tagore, letter to the Viceroy giving up his knighthood

official.text: Did the crowd at once start to disperse as soon as you fired? (A.) Immediately. (Q.) Did you continue firing? (A.) Yes. (Q.) If the crowd was going to disperse why did you not stop firing? (A.) I thought it my duty to go on firing until it dispersed. If I fired a little the effect would not be sufficient.
official.who: General R. E. H. Dyer, who gave the order to fire, questioned by the government's Disorders Inquiry (Hunter) Committee (as read out in the House of Lords)
official.date: evidence of 1919; read in the Lords on 19 July 1920

official.text: In continuing firing as long as he did it is evident that General Dyer had in view not merely the dispersal of the crowd that had assembled contrary to his orders, but the desire to produce a moral effect in the Punjab.
official.who: Majority report of the Hunter Committee, as quoted in the House of Lords (it goes on to call this a misconception of his duty)

disputed: How many were killed. The official British figure is 379. The Indian National Congress inquiry wrote that 1,000 was no exaggeration; other contemporary estimates ran from about 500 to over 1,000, and the historian Kim Wagner puts it between 500 and 600.
Whether the crowd was warned. The Hunter Committee held that notice to disperse should have been given; Dyer's defenders in the Lords argued that earlier proclamations were warning enough.
stories.blind: Most of the dead and wounded were never named in the record; they appear as numbers, and the story is told mainly through officials, commissions and famous protesters rather than the people in the garden.
reading: Jallianwala Bagh at 100: how many actually died (The Week)

stories.title: Peterloo
facts: On 16 August 1819 a meeting on St Peter's Field, Manchester, called by the Manchester Patriotic Union to demand votes for all men and fairer representation, was broken up by cavalry.
https://historyofparliament.com/2013/10/15/peterloo-and-its-aftermath/
The Manchester and Salford Yeomanry and the 15th Hussars were sent into a crowd of more than 60,000.
https://historyofparliament.com/2019/08/16/protest-against-the-six-acts/
The University of Manchester counts 18 people who died of injuries received that afternoon and up to 700 injured; the name Peterloo mocked the Battle of Waterloo four years earlier.
https://www.digitalcollections.manchester.ac.uk/collections/peterloo
The speaker, Henry Hunt, was charged with high treason, later reduced to sedition, and jailed for 30 months.
https://historyofparliament.com/2013/10/15/peterloo-and-its-aftermath/
By the end of 1819 Parliament had passed the Six Acts, restricting public meetings, arms and the radical press.
https://historyofparliament.com/2019/08/16/protest-against-the-six-acts/
John Edward Taylor, who was there and served on the committee for the victims' relief, founded the Manchester Guardian, first published on 5 May 1821.
https://www.digitalcollections.manchester.ac.uk/view/AR-GDN-00150-00001

voices.text: The cavalry were in confusion: they evidently could not, with all the weight of man and horse, penetrate that compact mass of human beings; and their sabres were plied to hew a way through naked held-up hands and defenceless heads; and then chopped limbs and wound-gaping skulls were seen; and groans and cries were mingled with the din of that horrid confusion.
voices.who: Samuel Bamford, a weaver from Middleton who led his town's contingent that day
voices.doc: Passages in the Life of a Radical, 1893 edition, p. 156 (transcribed from the scan; line-break hyphens joined)

voices.text: Many females appeared as the crowd opened; and striplings or mere youths also were found. Their cries were piteous and heart-rending, and would, one might have supposed, have disarmed any human resentment: but here their appeals were in vain. Women, white-vested maids, and tender youths, were indiscriminately sabred or trampled; and we have reason for believing that few were the instances in which that forbearance was vouchsafed which they so earnestly implored.
voices.doc: Passages in the Life of a Radical, 1893 edition, p. 156 (transcribed from the scan)

official.text: the seditious practices so long prevalent in some of the manufacturing districts of the country have been continued with increased activity since you were last assembled in parliament.
official.who: The Prince Regent's speech opening Parliament, which went on to call for measures to suppress them (the Six Acts); it did not mention Peterloo by name

disputed: How many were killed and hurt. The History of Parliament says at least 11 dead and 400–600 injured; UNESCO UK says at least 15 killed and 700 seriously injured; the University of Manchester says 18 dead and up to 700 injured, and that the magistrates' version seriously downplayed the casualties.
How big the crowd was: estimates run from about 60,000 to 80,000.
stories.blind: Most crowd testimony comes from men speaking in court or writing for reform. The many women at the meeting, and the injured too poor or afraid to claim relief, survive mostly as names and injury notes in the relief fund's records.
reading: Peterloo Relief Fund account book (UNESCO UK Memory of the World)

stories.title: The Myall Creek massacre
stories.where: Myall Creek, near Bingara, New South Wales, Australia (memorial site)
facts: On 10 June 1838 a group of armed stockmen rode onto Myall Creek station and killed Wirrayaraay women, children and old men of the Gamilaraay nation.
https://myallcreek.org/the-massacre-story/
The remains of at least 28 people were later seen at the site; the full death toll has never been confirmed.
https://nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/myall-creek-massacre
At the first trial, on 15 November 1838, all 11 accused men were found not guilty.
https://nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/myall-creek-massacre
At a second trial, begun on 29 November 1838, seven men were found guilty and sentenced to death; they were hanged in Sydney on 18 December 1838.
https://nma.gov.au/defining-moments/resources/myall-creek-massacre
The man who led the attack, John Fleming, was never tried.
https://mhnsw.au/stories/general/myall-creek-massacre/
On 10 June 2000 Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Australians opened a memorial at the site; it joined the National Heritage List in 2008.
https://apps.environment.nsw.gov.au/dpcheritageapp/ViewHeritageItemDetails.aspx?ID=5056626

voices.text: the mothers and children were crying, and the little ones that could not walk; Russel brought out he end of the rope that they were tied with, and gave it to one of the men on horseback; they then started, taking the blacks with them; the man who took the rope from Russel went in front; they were tied; one black was handcuffed; their hands were all tied, with the palms to each other; the rope was a very long one; they took all the blacks away, except two boys that jumped into the creek as the men were coming up
voices.who: George Anderson, the station's hut-keeper, giving evidence at the first trial
voices.date: 15 November 1838 (reported in the Sydney Gazette, 20 November 1838)
voices.doc: R. v. Kilmeister (No. 1) [1838] NSWSupC 105, Macquarie Law School (archived copy; the live site was not answering)

voices.text: There was here no provocation; no cause for anger. Men, women, children, even babes hanging at their mothers' breasts, not less than 30 altogether of these unfortunate defenceless blacks, who were quietly reposing by their evening fire, believing themselves safe in the friendship of one of you, were suddenly surrounded by a party of horsemen
voices.who: Justice William Burton, passing sentence on the seven men
voices.date: 5 December 1838 (reported in the Sydney Gazette, 6 December 1838)
voices.doc: R. v. Kilmeister (No. 2) [1838] NSWSupC 110, Macquarie Law School (archived copy)

disputed: How many were killed: at least 28 (National Museum of Australia), “not less than 30” (the judge in 1838), with victims' names still not fully known.

The size of the party and who escaped justice: at least 10 and possibly 12 stockmen (Friends of Myall Creek); ten besides its leader (Museums of History NSW). The leader, John Fleming, was never caught; four of the accused were never retried; the same party is reported to have killed 30 to 40 more people nearby.
stories.warn: The 1838 words are kept exactly as printed, including terms that are now offensive.
stories.blind: The record is almost entirely what white men said in court and wrote in the press. Aboriginal people could not then give sworn evidence, so the survivors and the victims' families are missing from it, and most of the dead are still unnamed.
reading: The massacre story (Friends of Myall Creek)
Myall Creek massacre (National Museum of Australia)

press.text: The whole gang of black animals are not worth the money which the Colonists will have to pay for printing the very documents upon which we have already wasted too much time.
press.who: The Sydney Herald, editorial on the colony's new protectors of Aborigines, written while the Myall Creek accused awaited trial (the newspaper, now the Sydney Morning Herald, apologised in 2023)

stories.title: The Armenian genocide
stories.where: Harput (today Elazığ), one of the towns deportations began from (approximate)
facts: On 24 April 1915 the Ottoman government arrested about 250 Armenian intellectuals and political leaders in Constantinople (Istanbul).
https://www.britannica.com/event/Armenian-Genocide
The U.S. ambassador, Henry Morgenthau, reported on 27 April 1915 that more than a hundred Armenians had been arrested and were being sent into the interior.
https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1915Supp/d1395
Armenians across Anatolia were deported toward the Syrian desert; many of those who reached it were held in camps where they starved, and massacres continued into 1916.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Armenian-Genocide
On 24 May 1915 the Allied governments warned that they would hold every member of the Ottoman government personally responsible for what they called new crimes against humanity and civilization.
https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1915Supp/d1398
In 2019 the U.S. House of Representatives passed a resolution commemorating the killing of 1.5 million Armenians from 1915 to 1923.
https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-resolution/296
On 24 April 2021 the U.S. President formally used the words Armenian genocide in his annual remembrance statement.
https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/04/24/statement-by-president-joe-biden-on-armenian-remembrance-day/

voices.text: All the people of C. started the same day. I think we were about 600 families. We had with us all our cattle and all our property. The first night we reached AU. and slept that night in the fields. The next day we passed many corpses heaped together under bridges and on the road; their blood had collected in pools.
voices.who: An Armenian woman deported from the Harput region on 4 July 1915 (unnamed in the publication; towns are shown only as letters)
voices.doc: Bryce and Toynbee (eds.), The Treatment of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire, 1915–16 (1916), Doc. 68

today.text: Türkiye does not deny the suffering of Armenians, including the loss of many innocent lives, during the First World War. However, greater numbers of Turks died or were killed in the years leading to and during the War.
today.who: Republic of Türkiye, Ministry of Foreign Affairs (the Ottoman government's own words from 1915 were not found in a source we could check)
today.date: as published on its website (checked November 2026)

disputed: How many died. Britannica gives conservative estimates of 600,000 to more than 1,000,000; the 2019 House resolution and the 2021 presidential statement say 1.5 million.

Whether it was genocide. Turkey's government says Armenians were relocated away from a war zone during a fight for survival, that deaths came from wartime conditions, disease, famine and banditry, and that there is no authentic evidence of a plan; it calls the genocide label legally unfounded. The United States and many other governments call it genocide, and Britannica says most historians have concluded that it fits the definition. Morgenthau cabled in July 1915 of a 'systematic attempt to uproot peaceful Armenian populations.'
stories.blind: The best-known survivor accounts were published by wartime Britain with names hidden; the Ottoman archives, and Turkish and Kurdish civilians' own experience of those years, are largely absent from these sources.
reading: The Treatment of Armenians in the Ottoman Empire (Project Gutenberg)
U.S. diplomatic records, 1915 (Office of the Historian)

witness.text: Persecution of Armenians assuming unprecedented proportions. Reports from widely scattered districts indicate systematic attempt to uproot peaceful Armenian populations and through arbitrary arrests, terrible tortures, wholesale expulsions and deportations from one end of the Empire to the other accompanied by frequent instances of rape, pillage, and murder, turning into massacre, to bring destruction and destitution on them.
witness.who: Henry Morgenthau, U.S. ambassador in Constantinople, telegram to the Secretary of State

stories.title: The Herero and Nama genocide
facts: The war in German South West Africa began on 12 January 1904 at Okahandja.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/German-Herero-conflict-of-1904-1907
On 11 August 1904 at the Waterberg, about 1,500 German troops under General Lothar von Trotha attacked an estimated 40,000 Herero, about 5,000 of them armed.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/German-Herero-conflict-of-1904-1907
Most Herero fled into the Kalahari toward British Bechuanaland; German patrols guarded the desert's edge, and many thousands died of thirst.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/German-Herero-conflict-of-1904-1907
Survivors were held in concentration camps; up to 80 percent of the prisoners on Shark Island, near Lüderitz, are estimated to have died there.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/German-Herero-conflict-of-1904-1907
On 28 May 2021 Germany's Foreign Minister said Germany would officially call the events a genocide and pledged €1.1 billion, stating that no legal claims for compensation follow from it.
https://www.auswaertiges-amt.de/en/newsroom/news/-/2463598

voices.text: We were crushed and well-nigh exterminated by the Germans in the rising. With the exception of Samuel Maharero, Mutati, Traugott, Tjetjoo, Hosea and Kaijata (who fled to British territory) all our big chiefs and leaders died or were killed in the rising, and also the great majority of our people. All our cattle were lost and all other possessions such as wagons and sheep. At first the Germans took prisoners, but when General von Trotha took command no prisoners were taken. General von Trotha said, ‘No one is to live; men, women and children must all die.’ We can't say how many were killed.
voices.who: Hosea Mungunda, headman of the Herero at Windhoek, statement
voices.doc: Report on the Natives of South-West Africa and their Treatment by Germany (Cd. 9146, 1918)

voices.text: In 1906 the Germans took me a prisoner after we had made peace, and sent me with about a thousand other Hottentots to Aus, thence to Luderitzbucht, and finally to Shark Island. We were placed on the island, men, women, and children. We were beaten daily by the Germans, who used sjamboks. They were most cruel to us. We lived in tents on the island; food, blankets, and lashes were given to us in plenty, and the young girls were violated at night by the guards. Six months later we went by boat to Swakopmund, and thence by train to Karibib. Lots of my people died on Shark Island.
voices.who: Edward Fredericks, headman of the Bethany Nama, sworn statement

official.text: Any Herero found within the German frontier, with or without a gun, with or without cattle, will be shot. I spare neither women nor children—I drive them back to their people or I will fire upon them.
official.who: General Lothar von Trotha's proclamation to the Herero (English translation by David Ciarlo, German History in Documents and Images; original in the German Federal Archives)

disputed: How many died. Britannica says about 75 percent of the Herero and half of the Nama; the BBC says up to 80 percent of the indigenous populations; the 1918 report put it at 60,000 or more.

The 2021 agreement. Germany calls its €1.1 billion a gesture of recognition with no legal claims attached and says Herero and Nama representatives were closely involved in the talks; a Herero activist told the BBC the offer was not enough, and a historian said many descendants felt excluded.
stories.warn: The 1918 words are kept as printed, including terms that are now offensive.
stories.blind: Nearly all the survivor testimony was gathered by a British wartime administration that wanted to keep the territory, and reached print in English through interpreters; women's and San survivors' voices are few.
reading: Samuel Maharero's letter to Governor Leutwein, 1904 (GHDI)

stories.title: The Bengal famine of 1943
facts: The government's Famine Inquiry Commission estimated some 1.5 million deaths above the normal level in 1943 and the first half of 1944.
https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.206311
Britannica puts the toll at some three million people, dead of malnutrition or disease.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Bengal-famine-of-1943
Rice imports stopped after Japan took Burma in 1942, and a cyclone in October 1942 damaged the autumn rice crop, though Britannica says these events had a relatively minor impact on the food supply.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Bengal-famine-of-1943
Under a military denial policy in 1942, rice and paddy judged surplus were removed from the coastal districts of Midnapore, Bakarganj and Khulna.
https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.206311
In the House of Commons on 4 November 1943, the Labour MP Frederick Pethick-Lawrence blamed inflation, saying food-grain prices had risen by 100 to 700 percent.
https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1943/nov/04/india-food-situation
The economist Amartya Sen, who saw the famine as a boy, later described it as an entitlement failure: people could not afford food, rather than there being too little food overall.
https://www.britannica.com/topic/Bengal-famine-of-1943

official.text: The cyclone and the partial failure of the aman crop were serious and unavoidable natural calamities. But after considering all the circumstances, we cannot avoid the conclusion that it lay in the power of the Government of Bengal, by bold, resolute and well-conceived measures at the right time to have largely prevented the tragedy of the famine as it actually took place.
official.who: Famine Inquiry Commission, the government's own inquiry, Report on Bengal (transcribed from the scan; three scanning errors corrected)

official.text: Meanwhile, the tragic tale of loss of life has continued and is still continuing. The death rate directly or indirectly due to starvation, for Calcutta alone, has amounted to some 8,000 between 15th August and 15th October. There are no reliable figures available for the outside districts, but I fear that in South-West and South-East Bengal, the figures may have been even worse than those in Calcutta. Even now that sufficient outside supplies for the Province seem assured, there will be for some time no diminution in the loss of life, until the organisation of distribution has effectively covered the whole ground.
official.who: Leo Amery, Secretary of State for India, in the House of Commons

official.text: The problem before them has throughout been one of high prices and of local shortage, both essentially due to maldistribution rather than to an absolute over-all total shortage for the whole of India.
official.who: Leo Amery, Secretary of State for India, on the Government of India's task, House of Commons

disputed: How many died, and how reliable the official record is. The Commission estimated about 1.5 million; other estimates run to about 3 million. The historian Madhusree Mukerjee, comparing the Commission's unpublished hearings with its report, found serious omissions in its rice-supply figures.

Nature or policy. A 2019 study of India's famines found that five of six major ones were linked to drought, but not 1943; the economic historian Tirthankar Roy argues that focusing on 1943 gives a skewed view of imperial responsibility and weighs climate and environment more heavily.
stories.blind: Most deaths were in villages where nobody counted them; the Commission judged the recorded figures an under-estimate, by about 40 percent for 1943. The famine's victims are almost silent in the official record: this card has no first-hand account from them yet, and we are still looking for one we can quote.
reading: Mukerjee, The Bengal Famine of 1943: An Appraisal of the Famine Inquiry Commission (EPW, 2014)

stories.title: The Highland Clearances
facts: The Clearances were forced evictions in the Scottish Highlands from the later 1700s into the mid-1800s, mainly to make way for sheep farming.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Highland-Clearances
On the Sutherland estates, around 1810 to 1820, thousands of families were evicted and resettled on coastal crofts to gather kelp or fish.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Highland-Clearances
In June 1814 the estate factor Patrick Sellar cleared the townships of a Strathnaver farm he was taking over himself.
https://www.communitylandscotland.org.uk/resources/jim-hunter-reflects-on-the-200-year-anniversary-of-the-trial-of-patrick-sellar/
Sellar was tried for culpable homicide at Inverness in April 1816 and found not guilty.
https://www.communitylandscotland.org.uk/resources/jim-hunter-reflects-on-the-200-year-anniversary-of-the-trial-of-patrick-sellar/
After the potato blight of the 1840s many Highlanders emigrated to the Lowlands, Canada, the United States and Australia, some with passages paid by landlords.
https://www.britannica.com/event/Highland-Clearances

The Napier Commission, appointed in 1883, heard about 800 people at 61 places; the Crofters Holdings Act of 1886 then limited evictions and brought in fair rents and secure tenancy for crofters, though not for landless cottars.
https://www.highlifehighland.com/archives/highland-archive-service/online-exhibitions/the-battle-of-the-braes/the-napier-commission

voices.text: I was present at the pulling down and burning of the house of William Chisholm, Badinloskin, in which was lying his wife's mother, an old bed-ridden woman of near 100 years of age, none of the family being present. I informed the persons about to set fire to the house of this circumstance, and prevailed on them to wait till Mr. Sellar came. On his arrival I told him of the poor old woman being in a condition unfit for removal. He replied, "Damn her, the old witch, she has lived too long; let her burn." Fire was immediately set to the house, and the blankets in which she was carried were in flames before she could be got out. She was placed in a little shed, and it was with great difficulty they were prevented from firing it also.
voices.who: Donald MacLeod, a Strathnaver stonemason, describing the 1814 clearance decades later (one witness's account; Sellar was tried over these evictions and acquitted)

disputed: Eviction or emigration. The historian James Hunter describes about 200 long-settled Sutherland communities destroyed by eviction; Eric Richards and others define clearance more broadly, including voluntary departure, and recent scholarship differs significantly from John Prebble's 1963 account of Highlanders forced into exile by chiefs turned landlords.
stories.blind: Almost all the evicted people's words reach us in English, through interpreters, clerks or later campaigners; very little survives in their own Gaelic, in their own hand.
